effect_estimate.comment: The paper conducts no original statistical estimation, synthesizing descriptive secondary figures across four historical-institutional country cases.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Comparative synthesis of secondary data across 4 country cases finds mixed outcomes of formal privatization and a critical, legally constrained role for small-scale independent providers: (1) England & Wales: post-1989 privatization (with £4.95 billion debt write-off and a new regulator) saw average bills rise by up to 50% at some companies without industry-wide productivity growth improving relative to pre-privatization; (2) Argentina (Buenos Aires 1993 30-year concession): water coverage rose from 70% (55% in poorer suburbs) to 83% by 1997, adding 1.98 million water users (from 5.76 million) and 1.16 million sewage users (from 4.66 million) by end-2000 with estimated aggregate consumer gains of US$1.33 billion, but outlawing private wells/cesspools forced mandatory connections, tariffs rose 13.4% in 1994, a 1997 prepayment revision incentivized investment delays, and affordability burdens fell on poor neighborhoods; (3) Côte d'Ivoire (SODECI private lease/management since 1959): connections grew from 4,000 to 380,000 across >400 localities (urban coverage 89% in 1990 to 90% in 2000), yet 22% of Abidjan households rely on independent providers/traditional sources, aided by SODECI licensing standpipe tank operators and installing boundary commercial connections for resale into unauthorized settlements; (4) Israel & Palestinian territories: state-owned Mekorot supplies ~two-thirds of water under the 1959 Water Law with new BOO desalination tenders initiating privatization, while ~150 West Bank Palestinian villages lack piped networks and rely on unregulated tanker vendors with variable quality and oligopolistic prices. Independent operators supply up to >80% of the market in many developing cities without subsidies but are constrained by the lack of legal recognition and independent regulation.

mechanism_certainty.comment: Appraised under the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework (ceiling = 2). Coded as 1 because the study presents descriptive historical and secondary statistics linking ownership, concession, monopoly/licensing, and regulatory structures to water/sanitation coverage and affordability across four countries, without primary direct empirical observation of the administrative mechanisms by the author.

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines monopoly utility jurisdictions and authorized vs. unauthorized service boundaries (service_area, tenure), abolition of private water ownership and shift from ratable property-value tariffs to metering (property), transfer of sector planning to private operator SODECI (planning), tariffs, connection charges, surcharges, and prepayment structures (fees), utility sanctioning of standpipe tank operators and boundary commercial connections for water resale into unauthorized settlements (accommodation), outlawing of private wells/cesspools and illegal operation of unsanctioned vendors vs. regulatory compliance (sanction), and consolidation/devolution or separation of municipal, regional, and water/sewerage agencies (institutional_fragmentation).

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: The paper is a comparative historical-institutional multiple-case study tracing legal, regulatory, and ownership evolution across four countries using secondary literature, official ministry/agency documents, and macro-historical statistics without primary human-subjects data collection or a systematic review search protocol; it therefore maps to the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework (with NONE as the closest alternative if viewed strictly as a non-systematic narrative review of four country cases).

evidence_quotes.quote: The development over time of the water supply and sanitation sectors in four countries is analyzed to reveal the changing role of the private sector.

In the case studies of Argentina and Côte d’Ivoire, foreign capital interests played a much larger role in the privatization processes, and particularly with the case of Côte d’Ivoire, privatization occurred much earlier in the development process than occurred in England and Wales, or is now occurring in Israel.
However, they are constrained generally by the absence of appropriate institutional and legal frameworks, including the lack of independent regulatory authorities.
have monopoly rights to water supply services within their area of jurisdiction, while the other operators frequently operate without any official legal sanction and in some cases, illegally.

At the end of 2000, an additional 1.98 million people were connected to the water supply network, up from 5.76 million at the start of the concession, and 1.16 million additional people were connected to the sewage network, up from 4.66 million (Aguas Argentinas, 2001).
